I really wanted Viking' offense to be ROIDS, remembering the StarCaps scandal of about fifteen years ago, where two Vikings were suspended for several games for having tested positive for a chemical agent, one of the effects of which was that it masked the presence of steroids; the chemical agent was a component in a weight-loss supplement called StarCaps. There was circumstantial evidence that the two Vikings guys (and several other players around the league) were all using StarCaps not to lose weight but to hide their roid use. The kicker was that the chemical agent was not listed as part of the ingredients of StarCaps, so the accused Vikings asked how they were supposed to know, and, if the league knew about the presence of the chemical, how come they never told the players? Plus, one of the Viking players actually did need to lose weight, and claimed he was legit using it to lose a few pounds. A "dualist" might claim that the Viking in question could be both on a diet AND juicing at the same time, beefing up while slimming down...

I saved my AIDOCTOR rant for a separate post. (Let’s be clear, I’m fine with it as a crossword entry, I’m just complaining about in IRL).Now, don’t get me wrong, I’m not at AI apocalyptic, I’m not worried about my job, and there are plenty of appropriate uses for AI in medicine as an adjunct to physicians or other providers. But this latest “innovation” is just the latest appalling development in a long trend of commercialization and cheapening of medicine. 

First were the incessant commercials hawking prescription drugs for everything from cancer to schizophrenia. Then the pop up grocery clinics with providers who have no knowledge of or access to your medical history. Then the “medical emergency” kits filled with antibiotics which are so dangerous on so many levels. And now the notion that you can get decent medical care from a faceless AI.

Folks, please don’t fall for this. There are dozens of things we can do to make medical care cheaper, more accessible and better quality with real human beings who actually care about you. Let focus on that, please.

Now for some trivia of my own:

Isn't it interesting how cultures and languages can differ while being also quite similar? In English the creature in a china shop is a bull. In Polish it's... An elephant. The Polish word for an elephant is "słoń" - the etymology is not clear , but it possibly has to do with our ancestors mixing up... Elephants and lions, neither of which they had seen (the Turkic word for a lion, arslan, seems to be the root of słoń). The whole expression is: słoń w składzie z porcelaną (skład is an outdated, 19th/early 20th century term for a shop, which survives in this expression only; the modern term is "sklep")

20 years ago or so most Poles associated MOHAIR, the Polish moher, with the cultural, political, social and religious phenomenon of "moherowe berety", mohair berets. It was slang for listeners of the far-right, ultra-catholic, misinformation and hate-filled radio station Radio Maryja (Radio Mary) - 90% of whom were millions of old ladies, all seeming wearing mohair berets. It was a demographic that swung some Polish elections...

I quite enjoyed seeing 程 in the clue for 8D. It immediately made me remember the somewhat poorly clued 19A from the Saturday puzzle for 12/6/2025:

[Chinese surname transliterating “Zuo”]
Answer: TSO

TSO is the 19th-century Wade–Giles romanization of the Mandarin reading of any Chinese character that is rendered (sans tone marks) as “zuo” in the Hanyu Pinyin romanization system that is now generally considered standard. Because a transliteration is a conversion from one writing system to another, and both TSO and “zuo” are already transliterations of a Chinese character into the Latin alphabet, it doesn’t make sense to say that one transliterates the other. A more accurate clue would have been [Alternate transliteration of the Chinese surname “Zuo”]. Several people noted this in the comments. At the time, I stated that the Times would never have gone with [Chinese surname transliterating 左], but I guess I’ve been proven wrong!

And the wonder of something that’s so often taken for granted -- that all these answers are seamlessly interlocked.  Have you ever tried making a crossword, even a mini or midi?  The skill behind this!

After two days of puzzle misery -- two days where I threw the incompleted puzzle at the wall -- finally a puzzle that was reasonably name-free enough for me to finish.  I found it hard in the  SUSHI BOAT (where I had SUSHI BOwl) section and pretty easy everywhere else.  Although I did want hIDES something-or-other at the SIDESTEPS answer (57A).

BULL IN A CHINA SHOP is a very nifty grid-spanner and I loved the clue.

Some thoughts:
MOHAIR is nice and soft, but is it "silky"?  For silky, I prefer, well, silk.  Or at least satin.

And to define ST PAT as the "star" of Green day is pushing it, I'd say.  Also, shouldn't the "D" of day be capitalized?

Finally -- a tip from AI-avoidant me.  To avoid the AI DOCTOR, and you definitely should!, ask your medical question and then follow it with "/Mayo Clinic".  Or "/Harvard Medical Journal".  Something like that.  You're welcome.

The latter is equivalent to the former by *decree*. My point is that this pattern is the very definition of what a logarithm is. Determining the base-10 logarithm of a positive number N means nothing more than finding the power to which 10 must be raised to produce N.

So the base-10 logarithm of 100 would be 2, because 10 would need to be raised to the power 2 to produce 100.

10 ^ 2 = 100, so we can just as well say log(100) = 2 in base-10.
